title: THE LOOK THAT LOVES… AND THE LOOK THAT STEALS
paragraphs: THE LOOK THAT LOVES… AND THE LOOK THAT STEALS
The Difference Between Desiring Your Spouse and Coveting Someone Who Isn’t Yours—and Why Jesus Cares About What Happens in Your Heart Before Anyone Else Ever Sees It
There is a kind of desire that can make your marriage warmer.
And there is a kind of desire that can quietly burn your marriage to the ground.
From the outside, they can look frighteningly similar.
A glance.
Attraction.
A thought that lingers.
A body responding before the mind has finished processing what the eyes have seen.
And perhaps this is where many sincere Christians become confused.
“Is it wrong for me to strongly desire my husband?”
“Is physical attraction to my wife somehow less spiritual?”
“If sexual desire can become lust, should Christians be suspicious of desire altogether?”
And then there is the question almost nobody wants to ask aloud.
“What exactly happens when I look at someone who is not mine…and something inside me wants more?”
Jesus takes us directly into that uncomfortable place.
Not merely into the bedroom.
Not merely into an affair.
Not merely into pornography.
Not merely into what your hands have done.
He walks straight into the hidden room of the human heart.
And He turns on the light.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you…”
Then Jesus says something that has pierced consciences for two thousand years:
“…everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
The Greek behind the crucial phrase is devastatingly precise:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pros to epithymēsai autēn.
It carries the idea of looking toward someone in order to desire/covet her.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say that recognizing beauty is adultery.
He does not say that every involuntary physical response is adultery.
He does not say that husbands must stop finding women attractive—including their own wives.
He goes after something deeper.
The heart that does not merely see…
but begins to take.
The eyes see a person.
Then fallen desire whispers:
I want that person for myself.
That is where the battlefield changes.
Because biblical sexuality is not ultimately about pretending human beings do not experience desire.
It is about where that desire is directed, what it seeks, and whether it honors the boundaries God has established.
Long before Jesus preached the Sermon on the Mount, God had already spoken about this hidden territory.
“You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife…”
Exodus 20:17.
The Hebrew verb translated “covet” is:
חָמַד — chāmad
It can describe desire, delight, or longing depending upon context.
That matters enormously.
Because the Bible does not teach that all desire is inherently evil.
The problem is not simply that the human heart can desire.
The problem is that sin teaches desire to reach beyond God's boundaries.
Coveting says:
God has not given this person to me…but I want what is not mine.
And suddenly Jesus’ words in Matthew become even more piercing.
Adultery does not magically begin when two bodies touch.
There can be a betrayal rehearsing itself long before the hotel room.
Long before the deleted messages.
Long before the secret meeting.
Long before anyone else discovers anything.
It can begin when the heart starts imagining ownership of what God has not given it.
That is the difference.
You can look at your wife and desire her intensely without needing to apologize for being married.
You can look at your husband and long for his touch without assuming holiness requires you to become emotionally or physically cold.
Scripture is remarkably unembarrassed about marital intimacy.
Paul tells married believers:
“Each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband.”
Then he says that husband and wife should fulfill their marital responsibilities toward one another.
The Greek emphasizes this mutual belonging:
ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα… καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα
Each man his own wife.
Each woman her own husband.
First Corinthians 7:2–3.
There is something beautiful there.
Not ownership in the abusive sense.
Not control.
Not coercion.
Not the idea that marriage eliminates consent, tenderness, patience, or sacrificial love.
Christian marriage never gives someone permission to exploit another human being.
Rather, Scripture places sexual intimacy inside a covenant of mutual faithfulness, responsibility, exclusivity, and love.
Desire says to your spouse:
I choose you.
Coveting looks outside the covenant and whispers:
I want them too.
Marital desire can say:
I want to know you more deeply.
Coveting says:
I want to experience someone God has not given me.
Healthy marital desire sees a whole person.
Coveting gradually reduces a person to what they can provide for your imagination.
And that is why pornography is so spiritually destructive.
It trains the eyes to consume people.
Swipe.
Look.
Use.
Discard.
Another body.
Another fantasy.
Another face.
Another secret.
Nobody has to know.
Except somebody does.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the most terrifying thing about Christ's teaching is also one of the most beautiful:
Jesus cares about the person you are becoming when nobody is watching.
Not because He enjoys catching you.
Because He loves you too much to leave chains around your heart simply because the chains are invisible.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that means.
Your spouse thinks everything is fine.
Your children have no idea.
Your church friends would probably be shocked.
Your browsing history has been cleared.
The messages disappeared.
The account has another name.
Maybe nothing physical ever happened.
And you have been comforting yourself with that sentence:
At least I never actually cheated.
But somewhere inside you, another voice has been asking:
Then why do I keep hiding it?
That question hurts.
Let it.
Not because shame can save you.
It cannot.
But because conviction can lead you to the One who can.
There is another danger here too.
Some Christians become so afraid of lust that they begin treating their own spouse like temptation.
Affection disappears.
Flirting disappears.
Tenderness disappears.
Playfulness disappears.
They become roommates who pay bills, raise children, attend church, and occasionally wonder where the fire went.
That is not the solution either.
The Bible contains the Song of Songs.
Think about that.
God allowed a book overflowing with romantic attraction, longing, beauty, exclusivity, delight, and marital love to remain inside Holy Scripture.
Biblical holiness is not the annihilation of desire.
It is the redemption of desire.
God does not merely want to make you someone who says no to adultery.
He wants to make you someone capable of saying a deeper yes to covenant love.
Yes to faithfulness.
Yes to tenderness.
Yes to pursuing your spouse again.
Yes to putting the phone down.
Yes to rebuilding what neglect damaged.
Yes to confession when secrecy has poisoned intimacy.
Yes to boundaries before temptation becomes opportunity.
Yes to running from what feeds fantasy.
Yes to seeing people as image-bearers instead of bodies available for mental consumption.
And yes…
sometimes repentance means admitting that the person threatening your marriage is not another man or another woman.
It is the version of you that you have been feeding in secret.
That is painful.
But Christianity was never built around protecting our favorite version of ourselves.
Jesus calls us to die.
Then He raises something better.
Perhaps you have already crossed lines.
Perhaps this article arrived too late to preserve your innocence.
You committed adultery.
You had the affair.
You became emotionally attached to someone else's spouse.
You sent the messages.
You watched what you knew you should not watch.
You fantasized.
You lied.
You hid.
You betrayed someone who trusted you.
And now perhaps you are reading words about holiness while carrying memories you cannot erase.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not:
Pretend it never happened.
The Gospel is not:
Adultery doesn't matter.
The Gospel is not:
Everybody makes mistakes, so forget about it.
Jesus takes sin far too seriously for those cheap answers.
The cross tells us sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
And the empty tomb tells us grace is greater than we dared to believe.
That is Christianity.
Not scandal hidden beneath religious clothing.
Scandal brought into the presence of Christ…
and met there by truth and grace.
Remember the people Jesus restored.
Remember the sexually broken.
Remember the publicly ashamed.
Remember the morally compromised.
Remember Peter, whose failure was different but whose confidence in himself collapsed spectacularly.
Jesus specializes in meeting human beings in places they never imagined their story would go.
But grace does not tell darkness that darkness is acceptable.
Grace brings us into the light.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
First John 1:9.
Not excuse.
Confess.
Not manage.
Confess.
Not rename.
Confess.
Not hide behind “everybody does it.”
Confess.
And then receive what pride can never manufacture:
mercy.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Maybe your marriage needs repentance more than another date night.
Maybe your spouse needs to hear you say, “I have taken you for granted.”
Maybe you need accountability.
Maybe an app needs deleting.
Maybe someone needs blocking.
Maybe the private conversation needs ending tonight.
Maybe the pornography has to stop being treated like an embarrassing habit and start being confronted as something discipling your imagination away from covenant faithfulness.
Maybe you need pastoral help.
Maybe you and your spouse need wise Christian counseling.
Maybe you have been trying to defeat temptation while secretly keeping its phone number.
Jesus used shocking imagery immediately after His warning about lust:
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
He was not giving Christians permission to mutilate themselves.
He was communicating the radical seriousness with which sin should be confronted.
In other words:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
You do not defeat a fire by keeping gasoline nearby for sentimental reasons.
And please understand something else.
If you are married, pursuing purity does not mean merely learning how not to want somebody else.
It also means learning again how to treasure the person standing beside you.
Look at your spouse.
Really look.
Not through comparison.
Not through pornography-shaped expectations.
Not through Instagram filters.
Not through memories of how they looked fifteen years ago.
Look at the human being who has lived life beside you.
The face that has aged while loving you.
The hands that have worked.
The body that may have carried children, illness, exhaustion, scars, stress, grief, or years you never expected to survive together.
Desire can mature.
Attraction can deepen.
Covenant can teach the eyes something pornography never will:
how to see beauty that cannot be consumed in seconds.
Your spouse is not merely a body available to satisfy you.
Your spouse is a soul entrusted to your love.
And the stranger you are tempted to covet?
That person is a soul too.
Not your fantasy.
Not your escape.
Not your secret possession.
A person made in the image of God.
Somebody else's husband.
Somebody else's wife.
Or perhaps an unmarried person who still does not exist for your consumption.
The Gospel changes the way we look at people because the Gospel changes what we believe people are worth.
Jesus did not die for objects.
He died for people.
And once you understand that, purity becomes something far more beautiful than gritting your teeth and trying not to commit adultery.
Purity becomes learning to see human beings through redeemed eyes.
Maybe you failed yesterday.
Come to Christ today.
Maybe you failed ten minutes ago.
Come to Christ now.
Repentance is not promising God that you will become strong enough to save yourself.
Repentance turns away from sin and turns toward the Savior who already knows everything you are ashamed to tell Him.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He rose from the dead.
Forgiveness is real.
Cleansing is real.
Transformation is real.
But grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
Walk out.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, do not turn the comment section into a place for graphic confession or details that belong in private pastoral care.
But you can simply say:
“No more hiding.”
Or:
“Jesus, purify my heart.”
Or, if your marriage needs prayer:
“Lord, restore what we neglected.”
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer fighting for purity.
Someone may pray for you without ever knowing your name.
Someone may finally stop pretending.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone righteous before God.
It does not.
But because somebody scrolling tonight may be one private decision away from devastating everything they love.
Your share might put truth in front of them before temptation puts opportunity in front of them.
Because temptation has an interesting way of making us forget what conviction once made painfully clear.
Come back when your eyes begin wandering.
Come back when marriage feels ordinary.
Come back when comparison starts poisoning gratitude.
Come back when secrecy starts sounding reasonable.
Invite your husband.
Invite your wife.
Invite your children who are old enough to understand.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the Christian who has become lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Because everyone needs to hear that Christianity is not a museum for people who never failed.
It is the proclamation that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Not as a replacement for biblical giving to your local church.
Not because anyone can buy God's blessing.
And never because financial support is required to glorify God.
Scripture says giving should be voluntary and cheerful, “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary generosity can help Christian ministry continue.
If this ministry has strengthened you, convicted you, encouraged you, or helped turn your eyes back toward Christ, you can support its continuing work here:
He wants you.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your marriage.
Your sexuality.
Your wounds.
Your secrets.
Your failures.
Your desires.
Your future.
All surrendered to Him.
Because the deepest question is not merely:
“Did you look?”
It is:
What is your heart learning to love?
Desire your spouse.
Treasure your covenant.
Guard your eyes.
Refuse to turn people into objects.
Run from what trains your heart toward betrayal.
Repent when you fall.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek help when the battle becomes bigger than your secrecy can handle.
And when shame tells you that your scandal has written the final chapter, look again toward the cross.
There hangs the One who already knew the worst thing about you…
and still opened His arms.
There is judgment against sin.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is forgiveness for the guilty.
There is cleansing for the stained.
There is resurrection after devastation.
There is a Savior who can take a story you thought was permanently ruined and begin writing something you never believed could exist again.
So tonight, before you desire what was never yours…
look again at what God has entrusted to you.
And before you hide another secret from the person sleeping beside you…
remember the Savior who already sees into the room nobody else can enter.
Because the most dangerous affair may begin long before two bodies ever touch—and the most beautiful restoration can begin the moment one broken heart finally stops hiding from Jesus.
